head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Even AND divisible by 3 is the same as divisible by lcm(2, 3) = 6

blocks.h: Why one test for 'even and divisible by 3'?
p: A number that is divisible by both 2 and 3 is divisible by 6, because 2 and 3 are coprime. `x % 6 == 0` is one check instead of two. The empty case returns 0 as the problem requires.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the filtered list (O(1) with running totals).

2455.takeaway: Even and divisible by 3 means divisible by 6: filter, then floor-divide the sum by the count.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Edges on the longest downward path from v
`-1` for an empty child, so a leaf has height 0
Nodes at depth d with their heights
Group nodes that compete for the deepest path on a level
Two tallest nodes on each level
Removing one node only matters if it is the tallest on its level, and then the runner-up takes over
New tree height if the tallest node on the level is removed
Depth of the level + height of the runner-up

p: Tree `[1,3,4,2,null,6,5,null,null,null,null,null,7]`, query: remove node 4 → [2].

Removing node 4 (depth 1): it is the tallest node on its level (height 2), so the runner-up on that level, node 3 (height 1), decides the new height: `d + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2`. Had the removed node not been the tallest, the answer would be `d + (height of the tallest node) `.

blocks.h: Why only the top two per level?
p: After removing q at depth d, any surviving node deeper than d must descend from some OTHER node on level d. So the deepest survivor below level d is at depth d + (the largest height among the other level-d nodes). If another node exists on level d, the new tree height is at least d, which beats every shallower node, so that is the answer. If q is the only node on its level, the deepest survivor sits on level d − 1, so the height is d − 1. To get 'the largest height among the others' for any q in O(1), it is enough to remember the TWO tallest nodes of each level: if q is the tallest, use the second, otherwise use the first.

bullets: Time: O(n + q) after one traversal and per-level sorting (O(n log n) for the sort).

2458.takeaway: Store depth and height per node and the two tallest nodes per depth: removing a node replaces it by the runner-up on its level.

rows: Counts of values in the current window
The number of keys = number of distinct values
Updated by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving one
Keeps `len(cnt)` equal to the distinct count

p: `Counter` keeps keys with count 0 after decrements, so `len(cnt)` would overcount distinct values. Deleting them makes `len(cnt) == k` a correct all-distinct test.

2461.takeaway: Fixed-size sliding window with a Counter: the window is valid when its Counter has exactly k keys.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: DFS (Depth-First Search) from Bob's node up to node 0
Records the time Bob reaches each node on his path (Bob walks the unique path to the root)
Bob arrives at u at time d
Set while unwinding the recursion, only for nodes on the path
Bob's time at u, or never
Nodes off Bob's path have no competition
Alice earlier → full amount; same time → half; Bob earlier → zero
Alice stops at a leaf: record the total

p: edges `[[0,1],[1,2],[1,3],[3,4]]`, bob = 3, amount `[-2,4,2,-4,6]` → 6. Bob's path to 0 is 3 → 1 → 0, so Bob's arrival times are `{0: 2, 1: 1, 3: 0}`. Alice's DFS:

Alice's profit at a node depends on who arrives first, so we need Bob's arrival times before simulating Alice. Bob's path is unique (a tree), so a first DFS finds it and records times. Alice may choose any root-to-leaf path, so the second DFS tries all of them, carrying the gain along, and keeps the best at leaves.

2467.takeaway: Two DFS (Depth-First Search) passes: record Bob's arrival times along his path to the root, then explore Alice's root-to-leaf paths with the first-come/half/zero gate rule.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Every subarray with median k must contain k
+1 for a bigger number, −1 for a smaller one
Balance of bigger vs smaller elements
Number of left extensions with this balance
Counter with `{0: 1}` for 'take nothing from the left'
Median is k when the balance is 0 (odd length) or 1 (even length, left middle)
Left extensions that make the total balance 0 or 1
Combine with the right side's balance

p: `[3,2,1,4,5]`, `k = 4` (at index 3) → 3. Left balances are counted first, then right extensions are matched:

In a permutation all values are distinct, so k's rank in the subarray is determined by how many numbers are bigger and smaller. For odd length, k is the median when the bigger and smaller counts are equal (balance 0). For even length, the median is the LEFT middle, so in a subarray of length 2m exactly m−1 numbers are smaller than k and m are bigger: the balance (bigger − smaller) is exactly 1. Splitting the subarray at k turns this into counting pairs (left balance, right balance) with a given sum, done with a Counter.

2488.takeaway: Balance of bigger minus smaller numbers around k: count left extensions in a Counter and match right extensions to total balance 0 or 1.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The smallest must pair with the largest, otherwise some pair would be too small
The i-th smallest and the i-th largest

blocks.h: Why must the smallest pair with the largest?
p: Every team has the same total T. Total skill = (n/2)·T, so T equals the average pair sum. If the smallest player were paired with anyone but the largest, that team's sum would be below the largest-with-someone team, making equal sums impossible. Sorting and pairing ends inward is therefore the only candidate, and the check verifies it.

2491.takeaway: Sort and pair the i-th smallest with the i-th largest; all pair sums must be equal.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Query indexes ordered by query value
Offline processing: smaller queries first, answers stored at their original index
The cheapest frontier cell is the next cell we could enter
The smallest frontier cell is below the query
If even the smallest isn't, we're stuck for this query
Cumulative: a bigger query can reuse everything a smaller one reached

p: The set of reachable cells only grows as q increases. Processing queries from smallest to largest lets one expanding region (a Prim-like frontier with a min-heap) serve all queries, instead of a fresh flood-fill for each. The frontier's smallest cell is exactly the next cell we can add once q exceeds its value.

bullets: Time: O(mn log mn + q log q).

2503.takeaway: Offline queries sorted ascending with a min-heap frontier: expand cells while their value is below the query and reuse the count.

A bitmask represents the SET of letters (duplicates don't matter)
Earlier words with the same letter set
Each earlier word forms one new similar pair
Add earlier matches, then register the current word

p: `['aba','aabb','abcd','bac','aabc']` → 2 (masks shown with 4 bits d c b a):

blocks.h: Why bitmasks and not sorted sets?
p: A mask is an integer, which hashes in O(1) and compares in O(1). `''.join(sorted(set(w)))` would also work but builds strings. Counting each word against the earlier ones avoids the double count of unordered pairs.

2506.takeaway: Represent each word's letter set as a bitmask and count earlier words with the same mask.

Sentinel: if still n, no match; any real distance is at most n/2

p: `['hello','i','am','leetcode','hello']`, target `'hello'`, start 1 → 1:

blocks.h: Why `best < n` as the final check?
p: The circular distance never exceeds n // 2, so initialising `best = n` means 'not found' is detected by `best` still equal to n. Returning −1 in that case avoids a separate `found` flag.

2515.takeaway: Circular distance to each match is min(|i − start|, n − |i − start|); take the smallest.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Fast modular exponentiation in O(log f)
Frequency of x goes from f to f+1: score changes by x^(f+1) − x^f
Update only x's term instead of recomputing the whole window score
Frequency goes from f to f−1: score changes by x^(f−1) − x^f
`0` when it reaches 0, since an absent value contributes nothing (and 0 would be `x**0 = 1`, which is wrong)
Take the modulus only when comparing
The running score may contain negative intermediate parts; Python's % returns a non-negative result
The problem asks for the maximum modded score, not the modded maximum

p: Recomputing a window's score needs O(distinct · log) work. Only the entering and leaving values change their frequency, so only their terms change: remove the old term x^f, add the new term x^(f±1). Each slide then costs O(log k).

2524.takeaway: Sliding window with an incrementally updated score: only the frequency terms of the entering and leaving values change.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: It may be chosen again later

p: Each operation adds the chosen number to the score and shrinks it for future use. Taking the largest now gives the most immediate gain, and the shrunk value is never larger than what the same index would have contributed had it been taken later. An exchange argument shows that using the biggest available value at each step is optimal.

2530.takeaway: Max-heap greedy: pop the largest, add it to the score, push back ceil(x/3).

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: +1 at the top-left corner of the rectangle
2-D difference array: only 4 corner updates per query
Cancel the +1 to the right and below the rectangle
Stops the effect outside the rectangle
Rebuild the real values by 2-D prefix sums
The difference array is the 'derivative' of the answer

p: n = 3, queries `[[1,1,2,2],[0,0,1,1]]`. Corner markers after both queries (before the prefix-sum pass):

blocks.h: Why not add 1 to every cell of each rectangle?
p: That costs O(area) per query, up to O(n²·q). With a difference array each query is O(1) (four updates), and one final O(n²) pass restores the values.

2536.takeaway: 2-D difference array: four corner updates per query, then a 2-D prefix-sum pass to recover the matrix.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of ways to choose f of the c copies of a letter (from `math`)
A subsequence is a set of positions, so positions of one letter are chosen as combinations
Either use the letter f times (choose which copies) or not at all
Remove the empty choice (no letters at all)
A good subsequence uses each present letter exactly f times

p: `'aabb'` → 11 good subsequences: 8 with frequency 1 (a, a, b, b and four `ab` choices) and 3 with frequency 2 (aa, bb, aabb). For each common frequency f:

blocks.h: Why does this count each good subsequence once?
p: A good subsequence has one common frequency f. For that f, every letter is either absent (1 way) or present with exactly f chosen positions (C(c, f) ways). Different f give different subsequences (their letter counts differ), so adding the per-f totals never double counts. The result agrees with a brute-force enumeration of all subsequences for `aabb`, `abcc`, `aaabb` and `abc`: True.

bullets: Time: O(26 · max frequency) combinations, each computed by `math.comb`.

2539.takeaway: Count by common frequency f: multiply (1 + C(count, f)) over the letters and subtract the empty selection.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: When we reach a pair, its nums2 is the smallest among all pairs seen so far, so it is the minimum of the chosen set
Min-heap of the chosen nums1 values
The heap holds the k largest nums1 values among the pairs seen
Remove the smallest nums1 when there are more than k
Score if the current pair's nums2 is the minimum
Sum of the k best nums1 × current minimum
Fewer than k chosen is not a valid choice

blocks.h: Why fix the minimum by sorting?
p: The score multiplies a sum by a minimum. Sorting by nums2 descending and treating the current pair as the minimum fixes the multiplier; then we only need the k largest nums1 values among pairs with nums2 at least that, which a size-k min-heap maintains in O(log k) per step.

2542.takeaway: Sort by nums2 descending so the current nums2 is the minimum; keep the k largest nums1 in a min-heap.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: New list of the rows sorted by the key
Key: negated score in exam k
Ascending sort of negatives = descending order of scores
Score of this student in column k

p: `sorted(score, key=lambda row: row[k], reverse=True)` is equivalent. Negating works only for numbers, while `reverse=True` works for any comparable key; either is fine here. Both are stable, so equal scores keep their original order (the problem says scores are distinct).

bullets: Space: O(m) for the new list of row references.

2545.takeaway: Sort rows with a key function on column k; negate the key (or use reverse=True) for descending order.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: A cut between marbles i and i+1 creates the pair of endpoints `w[i]` and `w[i+1]`
Each cut adds the last marble of one bag and the first of the next
Choose the k−1 cheapest or the k−1 dearest cuts

p: `weights = [1,3,5,1]`, `k = 2`: adjacent sums sorted `[4, 6, 8]`; k − 1 = 1 cut is chosen: max = 8, min = 4, difference = 4.

blocks.h: Why does the score reduce to cuts?
p: The first marble of the first bag and the last marble of the last bag appear in every split, so they add a constant to both maximum and minimum and cancel in the difference. Every other contribution comes from a cut: the marble at the end of one bag and the first of the next. Choosing k−1 cuts, the score is the constant plus the sum of the chosen cut costs, so the maximum takes the k−1 largest and the minimum the k−1 smallest.

2551.takeaway: Score = constant + sum of the chosen cut costs (w[i] + w[i+1]); the answer is the sum of the k−1 largest minus the k−1 smallest.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Taking v would exceed the limit
Every later number is larger, so none can fit either

p: To maximise the COUNT under a sum limit, always take the smallest available numbers: any selection of that size has a sum at least as large as the sum of the smallest allowed ones. The first number that doesn't fit ends the search since the rest are larger.

2554.takeaway: Greedy: take the smallest allowed numbers until the next one would exceed maxSum.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `sorted({b for b in banned if b <= n})`
Banned numbers inside the range, sorted and unique
Defines the allowed gaps between them
Sum of `mid` consecutive integers starting at lo (arithmetic series)
Largest count of numbers from this gap that fit in the remaining budget
Sums grow with count, so binary search works
The remaining budget can't buy any later number either

p: banned `[1,6,5]`, `n = 5`, `maxSum = 6` → 2. Gaps between banned numbers:

blocks.h: Why not loop over every number?
p: `n` can be 10⁹, so looping is too slow. The banned list is short, and between banned values the allowed numbers are consecutive, so their sums are arithmetic series. Within each gap a binary search finds how many fit. Another run, banned `[11]`, `n = 7`, `maxSum = 50`: answer 7 (all of 1…7 sum to 28).

bullets: Time: O(b log n) for b banned numbers.

2557.takeaway: Between banned numbers the allowed integers are consecutive: use arithmetic-series sums with a binary search per gap.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Can we rob at least k houses without adjacency using only houses worth ≤ c?
Take the house greedily and skip its neighbour
Greedy: taking the earliest eligible house never hurts
The answer is one of the house values
Binary search for the minimum feasible capability

p: With capability c the allowed houses form segments between too-valuable ones. Taking every eligible house as early as possible (and skipping the next one) maximises the number robbed, by an exchange argument (picking the first of two adjacent options leaves at least as much room). Feasibility is monotone in c, so binary search finds the smallest working value.

2560.takeaway: Binary search on the capability with a greedy non-adjacent count as the feasibility test.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Order of indexes doesn't matter, since pairs are unordered sums
Number of pairs with sum ≤ v
If `nums[i] + nums[j] <= v`, then `nums[i]` pairs with every element from i+1 to j
Sorted: replacing `nums[j]` by a smaller one only lowers the sum
Pairs with sum ≤ upper minus pairs with sum ≤ lower − 1
Inclusion–exclusion on a range: sums in [lower, upper]

p: Counting pairs whose sum falls between two bounds directly is awkward for two pointers, but counting pairs with sum at most v is easy. The pairs with sums in [lower, upper] are those ≤ upper minus those ≤ lower−1, with integer sums. Each count runs in O(n) after one O(n log n) sort.

2563.takeaway: Two-pointer count of pairs with sum ≤ v, evaluated at upper and lower − 1, then subtracted.
